newsitem.title: USA: Defense attacks Oklahoma bomb trial witness.
newsitem.headline: Defense attacks Oklahoma bomb trial witness.

text.p: The star prosecution witness in the Oklahoma City bombing trial faced a barrage of tough questions on Tuesday from an attorney for accused bomber Timothy McVeigh, portraying him as a drug user who could not be trusted.

But Michael Fortier, 28, a former army buddy of McVeigh's, held his composure as attorney Stephen Jones attacked his credibility, portraying him as coached by prosecutors and desperate to save his own skin.

Fortier had given damaging testimony on Monday that McVeigh planned the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City to avenge a government siege at Waco, Texas, two years earlier and spark an uprising among the American people.
The truck bomb, which killed 168 people, was the worst civilian attack on U.S. soil.

During Tuesday's questioning of Fortier, prosecutors revealed for the first time that the key to the rented Ryder truck believed to have carried the bomb was found three days after the blast in a nearby alley.
"Did you know they found the key to the truck in the alley?" chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler asked Fortier. "This is the first time I've heard of it," Fortier said.
Fortier had testified on Monday that McVeigh told him months earlier that he planned to park a getaway car in the same alley behind the YMCA building, a few blocks from the bomb site.

The discovery of the key in the alley would add credence to Fortier's account of what McVeigh had told him, undercutting defence claims that much of Fortier's testimony was based on newspaper articles he had read.

More than 90 government witnesses have testified, mostly about McVeigh's anger toward the government or how he allegedly planned the bombing. But the witness list has also included victims who focused on the human suffering caused by the blast.

On Tuesday, a representative from the Social Security Administration, Eric McKissick, testified about 16 employees and six visitors to the Social Security office who perished in the bombing. "The air was so thick you could almost chew it," he said in describing the scene after the bombing.

Jones asked Fortier if he been coached in "mock" court sessions, but Fortier said he would term the meetings "preparation." He said he had spent up to 175 hours with prosecutors and FBI agents since the bombing.
Fortier said he had met with Hartzler seven to 10 times, but insisted it was only to prepare for the trial and that he was telling the truth.
"Mr. Hartzler has never coached me on what to say," Fortier said, prompting Jones to ask if Fortier had been "coached" to give that answer. Fortier said "No."

"Wouldn't you agree, Mr. Fortier, that you have transformed yourself?" Jones said, referring to Fortier's clean-cut appearance in the courtroom, a sharp contrast to the dishevelled look he sported at home in Kingman, Arizona. "No sir, I wouldn't agree with you," Fortier answered calmly.

Fortier pleaded guilty to four felony counts, including knowing about a felony and failing to report it, in return for testifying that he knew about plans for the bombing but did nothing to stop it. He is in federal prison awaiting sentencing and faces up to 23 years in prison.
The defence has stressed that Fortier could hope to gain a much reduced sentence by pleasing the government with his testimony against McVeigh.
McVeigh pleaded not guilty to the bombing and faces the death penalty if convicted.

Jones showed Fortier three firearms transaction records signed by Fortier in which he certified that he was not a marijuana user, a condition for being allowed to purchase guns. "You signed it, a false statement made to the government?" Jones asked. "Yes, through this form," Fortier answered.
